subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Moments, levers, gears and pressure in fluids

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: A vector has both magnitude and direction, and force is a vector; mass, temperature and energy are scalars.

questions.q: A magnet attracts a steel paperclip without touching it. This shows that magnetism is what kind of force?
questions.explain: Non-contact forces such as magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces act between objects that are not physically touching.

questions.q: The weight of an object can be considered to act at a single point. What is this point called?
questions.explain: The whole weight of an object is treated as acting at its centre of mass.

questions.q: What is the unit of work done?
questions.explain: Work done is a transfer of energy and is measured in joules.

questions.q: Which equation correctly gives the work done by a force?
options: work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action)
questions.explain: Work done W = F s, where s is the distance moved in the direction of the force.

questions.q: When a force does work against friction on an object, what usually happens?
options: The temperature of the object rises
questions.explain: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store, raising the object's temperature.

questions.q: A force of 20 N moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
questions.explain: Work done = force × distance = 20 N × 3 m = 60 J.

questions.q: Which equation represents the force on a spring within its limit of proportionality?
questions.explain: Hooke's law states F = k e, where k is the spring constant and e is the extension.

questions.q: Which equation gives the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring (within the limit of proportionality)?
questions.explain: Elastic potential energy Ee = ½ k e² for a spring that is not inelastically deformed.

questions.q: Below the limit of proportionality, how does the extension of a spring vary with the force applied?
options: Extension is directly proportional to the force
Extension is inversely proportional to the force
Extension is proportional to the square of the force
questions.explain: Below the limit of proportionality the extension is directly proportional to the applied force, giving a straight-line graph through the origin.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m. What force is needed to produce an extension of 0.2 m?
questions.explain: Force = spring constant × extension = 25 N/m × 0.2 m = 5 N.

questions.q: Which equation gives the moment of a force?
options: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
questions.explain: The moment of a force M = F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

questions.q: What is the unit of pressure?
questions.explain: Pressure is force per unit area and is measured in pascals, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

questions.q: For an object to be balanced and not rotate about a pivot, what must be true?
options: The clockwise moment must be greater than the anticlockwise moment
The sum of the clockwise moments must equal the sum of the anticlockwise moments
There must be no forces acting on the object
The forces must all act at the pivot
questions.explain: The principle of moments states that a balanced object has total clockwise moment equal to total anticlockwise moment about the pivot.

questions.q: A force of 200 N acts over an area of 4 m². What is the pressure exerted?
questions.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area = 200 N ÷ 4 m² = 50 Pa.

questions.q: Which equation gives the momentum of a moving object?
questions.explain: Momentum p = m v, measured in kg m/s.

questions.q: Using Newton's second law, if the resultant force on an object doubles while its mass stays the same, what happens to its acceleration?
questions.explain: Since F = m a, acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force when mass is constant, so doubling the force doubles the acceleration.

questions.q: According to Newton's first law, what happens to a moving object if the resultant force acting on it is zero?
options: It continues at the same velocity
questions.explain: With zero resultant force an object stays at rest or continues moving at a constant velocity.

questions.q: The stopping distance of a vehicle is made up of which two distances?
questions.explain: Stopping distance = thinking distance (during the driver's reaction time) + braking distance (while the brakes act).

questions.q: A trolley of mass 2 kg moves at a velocity of 10 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explain: Momentum = mass × velocity = 2 kg × 10 m/s = 20 kg m/s.
